l4_steps.name: Monitor FAA/EASA AD publication feed
l4_steps.input: FAA ACAS / EASA AD database daily RSS feed
l4_steps.output: New AD log entry with urgency classification
l4_steps.kpi: AD logged within 24 hrs of publication; 100% capture rate
l4_steps.pain_point: Manual monitoring of multiple regulatory feeds (FAA, EASA, TCCA) creates gaps when engineer is on leave; no automated ingestion in legacy CAMP configurations

l4_steps.name: Classify AD urgency — Emergency, Priority, Routine
l4_steps.input: AD text, compliance deadline, subject system ATA chapter
l4_steps.output: AD urgency category assigned; emergency ADs flagged to Accountable Manager within 2 hrs
l4_steps.kpi: Emergency ADs escalated within 2 hrs of receipt; 0 missed emergency ADs
l4_steps.pain_point: FAA Emergency ADs may have 0-day compliance windows that conflict with active aircraft in revenue service, forcing AOG decisions without operational slack

l4_steps.name: Log AD record and open compliance tracking
l4_steps.output: AMOS AD record created with deadline, ATA chapter, and assigned engineer
l4_steps.kpi: AD record created in AMOS within 4 hrs of classification; 100% traceability
l4_steps.pain_point: Duplicate AD entries occur when engineers create records independently in AMOS and CAMP before integration sync runs, causing reconciliation rework

l4_steps.name: Pull aircraft configuration records for AD ATA chapter
l4_steps.input: AD applicability criteria (aircraft type, series, modification status)
l4_steps.output: List of tail numbers with configuration state for affected ATA chapter
l4_steps.kpi: Configuration match completed within 8 hrs; 0 tail numbers missed
l4_steps.pain_point: Config records in CAMP may lag behind actual installed mods if AMOS SB status is not synced in real time — risk of incorrect applicability determination

l4_steps.name: Determine fleet-wide AD applicability
l4_steps.input: Aircraft configuration records, AD applicability logic
l4_steps.output: Applicability determination: list of affected vs not-affected tail numbers
l4_steps.kpi: Applicability determination completed before 50% of compliance window expires
l4_steps.pain_point: Mixed-fleet operators with multiple sub-variants (e.g. 737-700 vs 737-800) frequently have partial applicability — manual cross-check against Boeing TASK data required

l4_steps.name: Evaluate AMOC or interim relief options
l4_steps.input: AD compliance method section; OEM service information; FAA AMOC precedents
l4_steps.output: Decision: accept standard compliance method or initiate AMOC request
l4_steps.kpi: AMOC evaluation completed within 48 hrs of AD receipt for routine ADs
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOC approval from FAA typically takes 30–90 days; if AD compliance window is shorter, airline must comply with original method regardless of cost impact

l4_steps.name: Submit AMOC request to FAA Aircraft Certification Office
l4_steps.input: Engineering justification, test data, equivalent safety analysis
l4_steps.output: AMOC submission reference number; interim relief authorization if granted
l4_steps.kpi: AMOC submitted within 5 business days of decision; FAA acknowledgement within 10 days
l4_steps.pain_point: FAA ACO response times vary by region and workload — AMOC approval is not guaranteed before original compliance deadline, creating dual-track planning burden

l4_steps.name: Create AD compliance work order in AMOS
l4_steps.input: Applicability list, compliance method, deadline from CAMP
l4_steps.output: Work order(s) created in AMOS linked to AD record, with task card reference
l4_steps.kpi: Work orders created ≥14 days before compliance deadline for routine ADs
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOS work order creation requires manual linking of AD record to each tail number — no bulk-creation tool for fleet-wide ADs affecting 100+ aircraft

l4_steps.name: Identify and procure required parts and tooling
l4_steps.input: AD task card materials list, current stock levels from AMOS inventory
l4_steps.output: Purchase orders raised; parts reservation against work orders
l4_steps.kpi: Parts confirmed available ≥7 days before scheduled maintenance window; AOG sourcing SLA 4 hrs
l4_steps.pain_point: OEM-only part requirements (no PMA alternatives) for certain ADs create single-source dependency — Boeing / Airbus lead times can exceed AD compliance windows

l4_steps.name: Determine maintenance venue — line vs hangar
l4_steps.input: AD task scope, aircraft access requirements, available maintenance slots
l4_steps.output: Venue decision: line maintenance window or heavy maintenance input
l4_steps.kpi: Venue decision confirmed ≥10 days before compliance deadline
l4_steps.pain_point: Line maintenance slots are constrained by turn-around times (~45 min); structural ADs requiring panel removal force unplanned hangar inputs, displacing scheduled C-check work

l4_steps.name: Schedule and confirm maintenance event
l4_steps.input: Maintenance venue, aircraft rotation schedule from Amadeus SkyWORKS
l4_steps.output: Confirmed maintenance slot; aircraft ground time blocked in ops schedule
l4_steps.kpi: Compliance event scheduled before 75% of deadline window consumed
l4_steps.pain_point: Aircraft rotation optimisation in SkyWORKS does not natively ingest AMOS AD deadlines — manual coordination between MRO planning and network ops required to protect ground time

l4_steps.name: Issue AD task card and brief certifying technicians
l4_steps.input: Approved AD task card, AMM references, special tooling instructions
l4_steps.output: Technician briefing completed; task card issued with required certifications noted
l4_steps.kpi: Task card issued ≥1 hr before planned job start; 0 tasks started without valid authorisation
l4_steps.pain_point: AMM revision cycles can lag behind AD effective dates — technicians may reference superseded procedures if Boeing Toolbox is not updated in sync with AD release

l4_steps.name: Execute AD compliance work per approved maintenance data
l4_steps.input: AD task card, AMM procedures, special tooling
l4_steps.output: Physical work completed; technician sign-off on task card steps
l4_steps.kpi: Zero rework rate due to incorrect procedure; work completed within planned man-hours ±10%
l4_steps.pain_point: Complex structural ADs (e.g. crack inspections under floor panels) can reveal findings not anticipated in original task card, requiring engineering disposition that extends ground time beyond AOG limits

l4_steps.name: Perform independent inspection and buy-back
l4_steps.input: Completed task card, physical inspection of work area
l4_steps.output: QA sign-off; AMOS work order buy-back recorded
l4_steps.kpi: 100% of AD tasks require independent inspection; QA buy-back completed before aircraft release
l4_steps.pain_point: Inspector availability at outstations is limited — line maintenance ADs executed away from main base may require ferry or mobile QA deployment, adding cost and delay

l4_steps.name: Record AD accomplishment in CAMP airworthiness log
l4_steps.input: Signed-off task card, QA buy-back confirmation from AMOS
l4_steps.output: CAMP AD compliance record updated with date accomplished, tail number, and next due date
l4_steps.kpi: CAMP updated within 4 hrs of task completion; 0 gaps in airworthiness record
l4_steps.pain_point: AMOS-to-CAMP sync is batch-processed overnight in some configurations — aircraft can technically fly after completion but CAMP still shows AD as open, creating audit exposure

l4_steps.name: Update aircraft technical log and maintenance records
l4_steps.input: Completed buy-back record, AD reference number
l4_steps.output: Aircraft technical log entry; AD compliance endorsement in journey log
l4_steps.kpi: Technical log entry completed before aircraft return to service; 0 releases without AD documentation
l4_steps.pain_point: Regulatory requirements differ by registry (FAA 14 CFR vs EASA Part-M) for how AD compliance must be recorded — dual-registry aircraft require parallel documentation in different formats

l4_steps.name: Assess FAA/EASA regulatory reporting obligation
l4_steps.input: AD text, compliance method used, any deviations or extensions granted
l4_steps.output: Decision: submit formal compliance report or retain on file only
l4_steps.kpi: Compliance reports submitted within 8 calendar days where required by AD text
l4_steps.pain_point: Not all ADs require formal reporting, but ambiguous AD language leads to over-reporting or under-reporting — both carry regulatory penalty risk under FAA Order 8900.1

l4_steps.name: Configure recurring interval alert in CAMP
l4_steps.input: AD next-due parameters (calendar days, flight hours, cycles)
l4_steps.output: Recurring alert configured; next-due dates visible in CAMP due-list dashboard
l4_steps.kpi: Recurring alerts configured within 24 hrs of initial compliance; 0 recurring ADs missed at interval
l4_steps.pain_point: ADs with multi-parameter thresholds (hours AND cycles AND calendar) require compound interval logic that CAMP supports but must be manually validated — error in threshold entry causes silent compliance gap

l4_steps.name: Generate AD due-list report for maintenance planning
l4_steps.output: AD due-list report distributed to maintenance planning and operations; items within 30 days flagged
l4_steps.kpi: Due-list report generated weekly; 100% of items due within 30 days actioned with work order
l4_steps.pain_point: CAMP due-list does not automatically interface with AMOS work order scheduling — planners must manually cross-check two systems to confirm no AD falls due during a planned revenue flight
